title: Tenancy pinning entropy and bandwidth leakage — notes
content:
Background:

This is a working note on a set of reproducible experiments and observations where multi-tenant pinning behaviours increase sustained NVMe and DRAM bandwidth use even when per-tenant request rates drop.

Motivation:
- We’ve seen production incidents where aggregate bandwidth rises and tail latencies worsen without a clear increase in RPS.
- Hypothesis: tenant-local pins (sticky residency) + skewed hotsets drive cross-tenant eviction resistance => increased paging and read amplification on SSDs.

High-level hypothesis and definitions:
- "Pinning" means model KV slots (page-sized residency units) that are preferentially kept resident for a tenant via heuristics (priority scores, recent-hot policy).
- "Entropy" here means the dispersion of ownership of resident slots across tenants. Low entropy => one tenant dominates residency. High entropy => many tenants fragment the resident set.
- "Bandwidth leakage" = NVMe or DRAM bandwidth consumed due to churn caused by eviction attempts that do not yield net reuse (measured as bytes read/sec that correlate with low subsequent reuse).

Quick reproduction recipe (local lab):
1) Build benchmark harness: workloads/multi_tenant_pinbench.py (attached to PR). Two tenants: T_hot (90% skewed seqlen=512), T_burst (short bursts, seqlen=64).
2) Start runtime with: --kv-resident-units=2048 --evictor-mode=hybrid --pin-threshold=0.75 --bank-throttle=off
3) Run T_hot at steady 350 qps, T_burst does 30 qps bursts every 60s. Collect: resident_ownership, eviction_events, nvme_read_bytes/sec, per-bank-utilization.
4) Capture runtime traces: ./tools/trace_collect --duration 10m --tags=kv,residency,io

Key metrics to collect:
- reuse_rate_per_slot (reuses / slot_lifetimes) sampled at 10s buckets
- resident_entropy (Shannon over owner distribution)
- eviction_futile_ratio = evictions_that_immediately_read_back / total_evictions
- nvme_read_bytes/sec and nvme_ops/sec (by instance)
- per-bank queue lengths and PCIe latency distributions
- tail latency p50/p95/p99

Observed behaviour (sample run, lab-2024-11-20):
- When pin-threshold=0.75 and bank-throttle=off:
  - resident_entropy dropped from 5.9 -> 3.1 within 5 minutes (i.e., T_hot dominated residency).
  - reuse_rate_per_slot for the dominated slots was high (~0.62) but for the long tail of recently-evicted slots reuse_rate ~0.04.
  - eviction_futile_ratio rose to 0.34 -> meaning ~34% of evictions were followed by an immediate readback within 30s.
  - NVMe read bandwidth increased 2.3x vs baseline; majority reads were small (64–256KB) and randomly distributed across LBA ranges indicating prefetched pages were not effectively reused.
  - p99 latency for T_burst rose from 120ms -> 420ms correlating with NVMe read spikes.

Interpretation:
- Pinning caused oversized residency for T_hot; when T_burst arrived it touched less resident capacity and caused eviction pressure. But because the eviction policy favored retaining pinned frames (higher score), evicted frames belonged to tenants with low near-term reuse, causing immediate readbacks when those tenants resumed. This creates a feedback loop: eviction->paging->readback->more eviction.
- The net effect is read amplification and DRAM bandwidth spikes (copy-ins) even if RPS didn’t increase substantially.

Experiment matrix tried so far (short summary):
- Vary pin-threshold in {0.3,0.5,0.75,0.9} -> higher thresholds reduce churn for the pinned tenant but raise eviction_futile_ratio for others.
- Enable bank-throttle (per-memory-channel cap) reduced NVMe bursts but increased per-request cpu context switches; p99 tradeoff observed.
- Introduced eviction-aging (time-decay on score) reduced eviction_futile_ratio by ~12% but increased 95th-listen-time in synthetic bench.
- Aggressive prefetch suppression for tenants with low recent reuse reduced read amplification substantially (NVMe read BW down ~28%) but increased first-token latency for cold-tenants ~40ms.

Commands and quick diagnostics (useful for oncall):
- curl http://metrics.internal/kv/resident_ownership | jq .
- ./tools/evict_trace_analyze --trace last_run.json --output heatmap.png
- edgestats grep nvme_read_bytes /var/log/serving/runtime_metrics.log | ts -s 1m

Proposed short-term mitigations (operational + config):
1) Alert: create rule "kv:bandwidth_leak_ratio > 0.25 for 5m" where bandwidth_leak_ratio = eviction_futile_ratio * nvme_read_bytes_norm.
2) Default pin-threshold to 0.6 on shared clusters; allow per-tenant override with caution.
3) Add sampled per-slot owner TTL: slots with owner with no requests for 90s should be demoted regardless of score.
4) Turn on bank-throttle for noisy instances by default in the Dedicated pools where NVMe is contended.

Longer-term code changes to try (design notes):
- Score hysteresis with ownership-aware penalties: when eviction would remove a slot owned by a tenant that has historical low reuse, bias eviction towards it even if its raw score is higher.
- Lease-based residency: give tenants a soft lease (window) that can be relinquished proactively if global reuse efficiency drops below threshold.
- Eviction impact predictor: lightweight ML model (logistic) using recent reuse_rate_per_slot + owner_traffic to predict eviction_futility and drive smarter selection.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What is the operational cost of TTL-based demotion (CPU and extra eviction churn) in high-RPS clusters? Need microbench.
- Where is the right balance between first-token latency for cold tenants vs overall bandwidth cost? Quantify dollar impact (nvme ops pricing) for customer-facing analysis.
- Gather a rolling 7-day histogram of resident_entropy across prod clusters to set sensible defaults.
- Instrument writeback/readback path further to distinguish prefetch-originated reads vs reactive demand reads.

Action items (owners):
- Alex R: add sampled resident_entropy metric to /metrics endpoint (due 2024-12-10).
- Priya N: run wide-scale sweep of pin_threshold values on staging and collect p95/p99 and nvme BW (due 2024-12-08).
- Kenji: prototype TTL demote patch and a unit microbench; open PR for review (due 2024-12-15).
- Maya: draft runbook for oncall to detect and remediate bandwidth leakage (due 2024-12-05).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic: the goal is to get reproducible signals and a few quick mitigations in before holidays. Long-term ML-driven eviction is interesting but not required for initial wins.
- Attached traces and harness code linked in PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/812

End of notes.
